title: Conservative Forces in Mechanics
short_intro: A conservative force is a force with the property that the total work done in moving a particle between two points is independent of the taken path. It depends only on the initial and final positions of the particle.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of conservative and non-conservative forces, path independence of work done, relation between conservative force and potential energy, conservation of mechanical energy for point masses.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Mathematical condition for conservative forces using vector differential operators (curl of force field is zero), scalar potential function derivation, central forces as conservative systems, Lagrangian and Hamiltonian mechanics foundations.

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Path Independence
bullets: A force F is conservative if the line integral of F along any path between two points A and B is independent of the path.
Mathematically expressed as the work done along a closed loop is identically zero: oint F • dr = 0.
Path independence implies that no mechanical energy is dissipated as heat or sound during the transit.

concept_notes.heading: Curl-free Condition (Differential Criterion)
bullets: A necessary and sufficient condition for a force field to be conservative in a simply connected domain is that its curl vanishes identically.
This implies that partial derivatives of force components satisfy exactness conditions, such as (∂F_x)/(∂y) = (∂F_y)/(∂x).

concept_notes.heading: Relation with Potential Energy
bullets: A conservative force can be expressed as the negative gradient of a scalar potential energy function U(r).
Mathematically given by F = -del U, linking spatial rate of change of potential energy to force.
The change in potential energy ΔU between two points is defined as the negative of the work done by the conservative force: ΔU = -W_{AB}.

concept_notes.heading: Conservation of Mechanical Energy
bullets: In a system where only conservative forces do work, the total mechanical energy E = K + U remains constant.
Any increase in kinetic energy K is accompanied by an equivalent decrease in potential energy U.
Non-conservative forces like friction violate this conservation by converting mechanical energy into thermal energy.

derivations.title: Path Independence to Zero Closed-Loop Work
derivations.conditions: Force field is conservative and continuous
steps: Consider two paths Path 1 and Path 2 connecting points A and B in a force field.
By definition of conservative force, work done along Path 1 (W_1) equals work done along Path 2 (W_2): int_{A}^{B} (Path 1) F • dr = int_{A}^{B} (Path 2) F • dr.
Reverse Path 2 to go from B back to A, such that work done along the reverse path is -W_2.
Combine the forward journey along Path 1 and the return journey along reversed Path 2 to form a closed loop: oint F • dr = int_{A}^{B} (Path 1) F • dr + int_{B}^{A} (Path 2) F • dr = W_1 - W_2 = 0.

derivations.title: Force as Negative Gradient of Potential Energy
steps: Define work done by a conservative force moving a particle from x to x + dx as dW = F(x) dx.
By definition, work done equals the negative change in potential energy: dW = -dU.
Equate the two expressions: F(x) dx = -dU.
Solve for force by differentiating potential energy with respect to position: F(x) = -dU/dx.

formula_sheet.name: Work Done by Conservative Force
formula_sheet.equation_html: W_{AB} = \int_{A}^{B} F \cdot dr = -\Delta U = U_A - U_B
formula_sheet.variables: W_AB = Work done, U_A, U_B = Potential energies at points A and B

formula_sheet.name: Differential Conservative Criterion (Curl)
formula_sheet.variables: F = Force vector field, \nabla = Del operator
formula_sheet.conditions: Differentiable vector field in simply connected region

formula_sheet.name: Force from Potential Energy (3D)
formula_sheet.equation_html: F = -\nabla U = -\left(\hat{i}\frac{\partial U}{\partial x} + \hat{j}\frac{\partial U}{\partial y} + \hat{k}\frac{\partial U}{\partial z}\right)
formula_sheet.variables: F = Force vector, U = Potential energy scalar function

formula_sheet.name: Conservation of Mechanical Energy
formula_sheet.variables: E = Total mechanical energy, K = Kinetic energy, U = Potential energy

formula_sheet.name: Gravitational Potential Energy (Uniform)
formula_sheet.variables: m = mass, g = acceleration due to gravity, h = height
formula_sheet.conditions: Near Earth's surface where g is constant

formula_sheet.name: Gravitational Potential Energy (Central)
formula_sheet.variables: G = Gravitational constant, M, m = masses, r = separation distance
formula_sheet.conditions: Zero potential energy set at infinity

formula_sheet.name: Elastic Potential Energy
formula_sheet.variables: k = Spring constant, x = displacement from equilibrium

formula_sheet.name: Exactness Condition in 2D
formula_sheet.variables: F_x, F_y = Components of force F

graphs_and_experiments.title: Potential Energy Well and Force
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A curve of Potential Energy U versus position x, showing minima, maxima, and point of inflection.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: At minima (stable equilibrium), dU/dx = 0 and d^2U/dx^2 > 0, so force F = 0 points back to equilibrium. At maxima (unstable equilibrium), d^2U/dx^2 < 0.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct questions on finding equilibrium positions and stability criteria.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Work Done Along Different Paths
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Two points A and B on a Cartesian plane connected by multiple curved and straight paths (Path 1, Path 2, Path 3) under a conservative force.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Work done integrated along Path 1 equals Path 2 and Path 3, demonstrating path independence.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual verification of conservative property in theoretical problems.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Conservative vs Non-Conservative Closed Loop Work
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A circular closed path on an F-r plane where a conservative force traces a loop, and a friction force trace on the same loop.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: For conservative force, area enclosed (total work in loop) is zero. For friction, total work in loop is negative and non-zero.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Distinguishing conservative forces from dissipative forces graphically.

solved_numericals.question: A force field is given by F = (3x^2 + 6y)\hat{i} + 6x\hat{j}. Show that this force is conservative and find the corresponding potential energy function U(x, y), assuming U(0,0) = 0.
solution_steps: Check the exactness condition: F_x = 3x^2 + 6y and F_y = 6x.
Integrate with respect to x: U(x,y) = -x^3 - 6xy + g(y).
Differentiate U with respect to y and equate to -F_y: -∂U/∂y = 6x - g'(y) = 6x ⇒ g'(y) = 0 ⇒ g(y) = C.

solved_numericals.question: A particle of mass 2 kg moves in a conservative force field described by potential energy U(x) = x^3 - 3x Joules. Find the positions of equilibrium and determine their stability.
solution_steps: Find the force or condition for equilibrium: F = -dU/dx = 0.
Set dU/dx = 0: 3x^2 - 3 = 0 ⇒ x^2 = 1 ⇒ x = 1 m and x = -1 m.
Test stability using the second derivative: d^2U/dx^2 = 6x.
solved_numericals.answer: x = 1 m (Stable equilibrium), x = -1 m (Unstable equilibrium)

solved_numericals.question: Verify if the force vector F = yz\hat{i} + xz\hat{j} + xy\hat{k} is conservative by evaluating its curl.
solution_steps: Write the curl expression: \nabla \times F = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \ \frac{\partial}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial}{\partial z} \ yz & xz & xy \end{vmatrix}.
Calculate the i-component: \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(xy) - \frac{\partial}{\partial z}(xz) = x - x = 0.
Calculate the j-component: \frac{\partial}{\partial z}(yz) - \frac{\partial}{\partial x}(xy) = y - y = 0.
Calculate the k-component: \frac{\partial}{\partial x}(xz) - \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(yz) = z - z = 0.
Since \nabla \times F = 0\hat{i} + 0\hat{j} + 0\hat{k}, the force field is conservative.

assumptions_and_limitations: The domain of the force field must be simply connected for the vanishing curl condition to guarantee path independence.

common_misconceptions.wrong: All central forces are necessarily conservative.
common_misconceptions.correct: Central forces are conservative only if their magnitude depends solely on the distance r from the center, i.e., F = f(r)r_hat.
common_misconceptions.why: Velocity-dependent central forces, such as magnetic Lorentz forces or drag forces directed towards a center, are non-conservative.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Friction is a conservative force because work done in a round trip is zero.
common_misconceptions.correct: Friction is non-conservative; work done by friction along a closed loop is always negative and non-zero.
common_misconceptions.why: Friction always opposes motion, continuously dissipating mechanical energy into thermal energy.

quick_revision: A force is conservative if and only if oint F • dr = 0 or ∇ × F = 0.
Work Done by Conservative Force: W_{AB} = \int_{A}^{B} F \cdot dr = -\Delta U = U_A - U_B
